title: Growing wild garlic
subtitle: A native woodland allium that colonises shady ground and provides a spring harvest.
excerpt: Wild garlic spreads to fill shaded ground under trees and in damp woodland edges, producing garlicky leaves in March and April. Let it naturalise in a shady corner and it becomes self-maintaining. The leaves, flowers, and bulbs are all edible.
sourceNotes: Species information from Flora of the British Isles (Clapham, Tutin, Warburg, 1952). Cultivation notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). UK edibility notes widely documented in foraging and kitchen garden literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Planting bulbs or perennials to spread and establish of their own accord, without annual replanting. Wild garlic, snowdrops, and bluebells are commonly naturalised in shaded areas. A naturalised planting requires no routine management once established.

content.text: Wild garlic (Allium ursinum) is a native UK bulb that fills damp, shaded ground in early spring. The leaves emerge in March and have a strong garlic flavour. By late May the plant is dormant and the ground is bare again. It suits the base of a forest garden, under trees, or in any damp, shaded patch where little else will grow.

Plant bulbs in September to October in groups of five to ten, 5 cm deep, 10 cm apart. Plant in shade or partial shade in moist, leafy soil. Wild garlic can also be grown from seed, but seed germinates the following spring and the plant takes two to three years to reach a harvestable size. Bulbs are much faster.
. The bulbs multiply and the plant self-seeds. A small initial planting expands to fill the available shaded area within four to five years.

Pick individual leaves from March onwards, leaving most of the plant intact to build root reserves. The young flower buds in April are edible and have a stronger flavour than the leaves. The white flowers in May are edible in salads. Harvest no more than a third of the leaves from any clump in a season.

attrs.title: Confirming the plant
attrs.body: Wild garlic can grow alongside lily of the valley, which is poisonous. Bruise or tear a leaf: wild garlic smells strongly of garlic; lily of the valley has no garlic smell. Always check before eating.
